newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel aims to clear air with Turkey's Islamist PM.
newsitem.headline: Israel aims to clear air with Turkey's Islamist PM.

text.p: Israel's Foreign Minister David Levy said he aimed during a visit starting on Tuesday to clear the air with Turkey's Islamist prime minister, a persistent critic of ties with the Jewish state.
Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan agreed to meet Levy only after Israel's embassy in Ankara publicly voiced frustration at his lack of response to its request for a meeting.
"His stance will be heard. He will also hear our stance," said Levy, whose two-day visit is the first high-level trip since both countries formed new governments last June.

Levy pointed out that Turkey -- Israel's main Middle East trading partner -- had just last week given parliamentary ratification to a free-trade accord. He will be accompanied by businessmen on the largely economic mission.

"Only a couple of days ago the parliament overwhelmingly approved the free-trade accord with Israel which even his (Erbakan's) party -- that is the coalition -- supported," Levy told Israeli army radio.
"So I will try to lift clouds and restore relations and a good and open dialogue also to the satisfaction of Prime Minister Erbakan," he said.

Levy will meet Turkish officials on investments and joint ventures at a time of growing defence, commercial and political links. He will also meet Foreign Minister Tansu Ciller of the coalition's secularist wing and President Suleyman Demirel.
He will meet Jewish leaders in Istanbul.

Israel said on Monday that trade with Turkey could quadruple to $2 billion by the year 2000 under the free-trade accord. It said trade in 1996 stood at around $450 million, of which $196 million was in exports and $252 million in imports.

Turkey's powerful armed forces, keen to expand cooperation with Israel, have been locked in a war of words with Erbakan, charging him with overseeing a creeping Islamisation of life in the officially secular republic.

In his election campaign Erbakan urged renouncing a training pact with Israel, signed by the Turkish army's number two man. The deal remains in effect despite the public opposition of Erbakan's Islam-based Welfare Party.

Under the military deal, which angered Iran, most of the Arab world and some Islamists in Turkey, Israeli jets train over the Anatolian heartland, minutes from Israel's arch-foe Syria. Israel is also upgrading Turkey's ageing F-4 jets.
